characteristics.oxidation: Post-fermentation (accelerated wet piling and/or natural aging)
characteristics.harvestSeason: Summer and autumn (mature leaves are typically used)

description.short: Dark post-fermented tea with a characteristic nutty/'betel nut' aroma, traditionally packed into large woven bamboo baskets
description.overview: One of China's oldest dark teas (Hei Cha) and historically an indispensable commodity for Chinese migrant laborers in Southeast Asia. While sharing wet-piling principles with Shou Pu-erh, Liu Bao possesses its own distinctive betel nut and aged aroma.
description.leaf: Dark brown, often compressed into large woven bamboo baskets (longbao) or pressed into bricks
description.liquor: Deep ruby-red, almost black, clear liquor
description.aroma: Nutty, earthy, with a signature note described by locals as 'betel nut aroma' (binglang xiang)
description.taste: Smooth, mellow, earthy, free of harsh astringency, with comforting nutty depth
description.processing: Harvesting → withering → kill-green → rolling → post-fermentation (wet piling similar to wo dui) → aging in large bamboo baskets or pressing → natural maturation in aging cellars

history.origin: Produced in Cangwu County for centuries, taking its name from the historic tea trading township of Liubao.
history.development: During the 19th and 20th centuries, it became a primary export along the 'Tea-Boat Road' to the Chinese diaspora in Malaysia, Singapore, and across Southeast Asia, valued as an affordable, revitalizing beverage for miners and laborers enduring heat and demanding physical work.
history.modern: In recent decades, Liu Bao has experienced a strong domestic revival across China as a prized alternative to Pu-erh, especially among tea collectors seeking exceptional aging potential.
interestingFacts: The massive woven bamboo basket (longbao) used to age Liu Bao is the signature packaging of this tea, setting it apart from typical Pu-erh cakes and bricks.
Historically associated with tin miners in Southeast Asia, who relied on Liu Bao to stave off the humid tropical heat and support digestion.
